text: The wholesalers set the price of the catch, and the men who hauled it in have no say in the number. One family in a Sicilian village mortgages what it owns to buy a boat and sell the fish direct. Visconti gives this 160 minutes, and the length is the argument: debt does not arrive as a scene, it accumulates across a season of weather, meals, and small deferred repairs. The village speaks Sicilian, and the faces belong to people who actually fish, which makes the household less a subject than a cast. Brothers and sisters who never voted on the decision live inside its consequences anyway. It sits on 100 film italiani da salvare. What stays afterwards is smaller than any of that: the sound of a rope, a doorway crowded with relatives, a price nobody at the table controls.

A parcel of film reels arrives in the post, and the man who opens it has been losing track of which images belong to the world. José Sirgado makes horror pictures on almost no money, and heroin has flattened the distance between what he shoots and what he sees. The sender is Pedro, an obsessive of the same kind, who films for reasons neither man can state plainly. Caimán: 100 mejores películas del cine español keeps a place for it, though Arrebato behaves like something passed hand to hand rather than listed. Zulueta treats a camera as an appetite rather than an instrument, something that takes frames out of a person the way a habit takes hours. His horror is a matter of temperament, not incident: 110 minutes of rented rooms, tape recorders, red light, and a pulse that slows exactly where a thriller would tighten.

In 1902 a rocket is loaded into the barrel of a cannon and fired at the Moon, and the whole journey lasts fifteen minutes. Professor Barbenfouillis and five colleagues from the Academy of Astronomy make the trip, and the caves beneath the lunar surface turn out to be occupied. Méliès worked from the stage — painted flats, trapdoors, bodies that vanish on a cut — and the interest lies in watching a magician conclude that the frame itself can be the trick. Plausibility is never the aim. The astronomers travel in frock coats, the expedition is academy business before it is science fiction, and the Moon has terrain, residents, and a temper. Adventure, history, and science fiction are all filed against it, which mostly means the categories arrived afterwards. Fifteen minutes, and not one of them spent making the impossible look difficult.

Mogador, late in the 1920s, and the cabaret's audience is mostly Legionnaires with leave and nowhere to spend it. The singer newly arrived from Paris has stopped expecting much from songs or from soldiers. Von Sternberg builds the picture out of what light does to smoke, gauze, and a face held a beat too long: 92 minutes in which the camera is plainly more interested in atmosphere than in incident, and the romance advances by refusals rather than declarations. Made in 1930, when recorded sound was still a new weight on a scene, it treats silence as something to hold rather than fill. The Legion offers the man a life of always moving on. The club offers the woman a life of being looked at. Neither is offered as a trap, and neither as a rescue.

Sixty-four minutes, which for a feature is barely anything, and most of it concerns a young animal being looked at by a crowd. Dumbo is born with ears that draw comment, and the circus around him runs on comment: the tent, the parade, the acts that need an audience. His ally is a mouse called Timothy, smaller still, whose entire usefulness is in what he says. The 1941 animation is unfussy — flat washes of colour, weather that arrives in a few strokes, elephants drawn as weight rather than detail — and that economy suits a story about a body refusing to do what it is told. The score took an Academy Award and carries more of the telling than the dialogue does. What lingers is how casual the cruelty is: the kind a workplace produces without anyone deciding to.

A fisherman who has stopped wanting to live comes to a country pastor for help, which is the one situation the pastor's training was supposed to cover. There is also a woman who loves him and has said so. Bergman gives all of it eighty minutes and a Swedish winter, where the daylight arrives late, leaves early, and never quite fills a room; most of the film is two people sitting down and one of them having to speak first. Dialogue moves at the speed of reluctance. Nothing is staged that could be said instead, and little is said that the speaker is certain of. Nattvardsgästerna is the Swedish title, and the church calendar in it is not decoration: the services keep happening on schedule regardless of who believes what.

Keaton plays a young man going home, which sounds like the least dangerous errand available. He falls for a woman met on the way, and remains ignorant of the fact organising everything around him: her family has sworn to kill every member of his. Seventy-three minutes, and the threat is credible enough that the picture is filed as a thriller as well as a comedy. Nothing is ever signalled as a joke. He simply plays a man solving practical problems — how to cross a room, how to stay on a moving thing, how to be polite — while the audience holds what he does not. The gags are engineering, worked out in real space at real risk, framed wide and held long enough that no cut can be suspected of doing the labour. Romance and mortal threat share the same rooms, and neither is played down to accommodate the other.

The entire event is one day out of Paris, an inn in the country, and a family with nothing to do until evening. Renoir needs forty-one minutes for it. The daughter falls in love with a man at the inn, and the film's interest is not in whether that is wise but in how fast an afternoon becomes the one that later afternoons get measured against. Weather does much of the work: wind in the grass, a sky changing its mind. The class comedy is quiet and unsparing — townspeople performing a leisure they have had no practice at, in a countryside that owes them no cooperation. Nothing at this length is explained twice. Cahiers du Cinéma: 100 plus beaux films du monde carries it, and the forty-one minutes never feel like an excerpt.

A rumour costs nothing to start, and in a seventeenth-century Kyoto household it cannot be taken back. The scrollmaker's wife is said to have gone to his most trusted employee. It is untrue, and that changes nothing: the two leave the city together, and the cold elegance of Mizoguchi's film is that the accusation runs ahead of them until it is no longer false. He works in long gliding takes that keep the order of a room visible — who kneels, who stands, who sits nearest the door — so that every conversation is also a diagram of rank. 102 minutes, patient rather than slow. The pressure is procedural: a house that must be seen to behave correctly, and a city where correctness is everybody's business. Nothing here is punished for being loud.

Seven test pilots, one new programme, and a country that needed the photographs as much as the flights. Kaufman covers the beginning of the American space effort by refusing the compression a shorter film would need: the selection, the physicals, the waiting, the press conferences, none of it reduced to montage, all of it weighted the same as flight. Three hours and thirteen minutes, and a great deal of it happens on the ground. The distance the film keeps measuring is between the men who could fly and the men who could be presented. The cinematography took an Academy Award and earns the length — wide dry light, aircraft filmed as machinery rather than symbol, altitude conveyed by how little there is left to see. It is comic about the salesmanship and serious about the nerve, and never asks for a choice between them.

The soldiers are shipping out, so the town throws a party, and one small-town girl with a weakness for uniforms wakes the next morning married to a man she cannot name. That is the situation Sturges handed himself in 1943, in a country at war and a studio system with firm ideas about what a comedy may contain; much of the writing is a feat of saying things without stating them. The dialogue overlaps, doubles back, and outruns every character trying to keep up with it. Around the girl stands a small town, which here means a chorus of relatives, officials, and neighbours with a stake in her respectability. The screenplay took an Academy Award. What holds up is the machinery underneath: everybody is decent, nobody is calm, and each solution manufactures two more problems.

Irma Vep belongs to an organisation the Paris police cannot locate, let alone charge. Ten episodes, seven hours, 1915: Feuillade had room to let a criminal gang become a fact of the city rather than a case to be solved. A journalist, Philippe Guérande, appoints himself the investigator, which in a serial means the story can afford to lose him and find him again. The pleasure is procedural and cumulative — disguises, trapdoors, coded messages, a reach that is assumed rather than proved. The form teaches itself as it goes: cliffhanger, recap, escalation. And the city carries much of it, a Paris of courtyards, staircases, and rooftops where any building might have a second use.

Veterinary school opens with a week of hazing, and Justine, who has never eaten meat, is expected to swallow what the older students put in front of her. Ducournau films the campus as a closed system — dormitories, corridors, caged animals, rules nobody wrote down — so the first act is about conformity long before it is about appetite. A rule broken once stops being a rule, and the change in Justine starts as embarrassment and does not stay there. The film is exact about physical detail in a way that is hard to sit through and never idle, and it is funny about student life in the same minute. The direction took a César. Ninety-eight minutes, no wasted scene, and horror that stays interested in the girl rather than the effect.

The film says at the outset that there is much ugliness in the world, and then spends twenty-one minutes looking at a leper colony in the north of Iran. Forugh Farrokhzad sets prayer and gratitude directly against the faces of people whose illness cannot be hidden, and the tension held throughout is between what is recited aloud and what is on screen while it is being recited. Nobody in it is presented as a case study. The routines are ordinary — meals, work, treatment, waiting — and the camera is neither clinical nor pitying, which is a harder position to hold than it sounds. The commentary is written to be spoken rather than to inform; the images do not illustrate it, and it does not explain them. Twenty-one minutes, and none of them decorative.
